references.text: Addresses rules about who may participate in the Passover meal, including slaves purchased with money, showing that bought slaves had a different status than foreigners.
Gives laws concerning Hebrew slaves and their rights, which stand in contrast to the rules for slaves from foreign nations in Leviticus 25:44.
Describes how people from distant cities could be forced into labor, related to acquiring slaves from surrounding nations.
Prophesies a future reversal where Israel will own those who held them as slaves, using similar terminology for slaves and servants.
Mentions Tyre's trade in humans as slaves, including from various nations, illustrating the practice of buying slaves from foreign peoples.
Condemns the selling of Judah's and Jerusalem's children to the Greeks, showing abuse of slave practices involving foreign nations.
Paul gives instructions to slaves and masters in the context of the new covenant, showing how the relationship between slaves and masters was understood in New Testament times.
Provides guidelines for slaves and masters in Christian households, reflecting the social reality of slavery that also forms the background for Leviticus 25:44.
